article.headline: A New CLI Lets Agents Control Browsers by Writing Code
article.lede: Most AI browser-automation tools work by showing the agent screenshots and asking it to click things. Sawyer Hood's `dev-browser` cli bets on a different architecture: let the agent write and run code against the browser directly, skipping the visual back-and-forth entirely. The result, he claims, is the fastest path to agent-controlled browsing available today.
article.body:
The dominant paradigm for giving AI agents a browser — tools like computer-use or most Playwright wrappers — works by capturing a screenshot, sending it to the model, receiving an action ("click at coordinate 240, 180"), executing that action, screenshotting again, and repeating. Each loop costs a round-trip to the model and a full image token payload. For anything beyond a few clicks, the latency and cost add up quickly.

`dev-browser` sidesteps this loop by treating the browser as a **code execution environment** rather than a visual surface. The agent is given tools to write code — JavaScript, Playwright calls, or equivalent — that runs directly in or against the browser, rather than narrating its way through a UI frame by frame. One well-formed script can accomplish what might otherwise take a dozen screenshot cycles.

The demo in the image makes the proposition concrete. Hood asks Claude Code to "use dev-browser to connect to my Chrome and create a Google Sheet of popular movies." The agent does it in a single composed action visible in the terminal, with no screenshot carousel in sight. Connecting to a *running* Chrome instance (rather than spawning a headless one) is significant: it means the agent inherits the user's existing session, cookies, and login state — no re-authentication required.

The install path is deliberately frictionless: `npm i -g dev-browser`, then instruct your agent to "use dev-browser." That phrasing suggests the tool ships with an *MCP server* or similar integration layer that Claude Code and comparable agents can discover automatically, rather than requiring custom tool-call scaffolding from the developer.

No research sources were available to confirm implementation details — architecture specifics, whether it uses the *Chrome DevTools Protocol* (*CDP*) under the hood, or how it sandboxes agent-generated code — so those claims rest solely on what the tweet and image show. What is clear is that the code-first framing is a deliberate design statement in a crowded field where screenshot-based agents remain the default.

concepts.definition: A pattern where an AI agent is shown a screenshot of the current browser state, decides on an action (click, type, scroll), executes it, then receives a new screenshot and repeats. Each iteration requires a full model inference call, making complex tasks slow and expensive.

An alternative to screenshot loops in which the agent writes executable code — JavaScript, Playwright commands, or similar — that acts on the browser directly. A single script can perform many actions in one shot, dramatically reducing round-trips to the model.

An API built into Chromium-based browsers that allows external programs to inspect, debug, and control the browser programmatically. Tools like Playwright and Puppeteer use CDP under the hood; connecting via CDP to a live browser lets an agent operate within an existing authenticated session.

Short for Model Context Protocol server — a small integration layer that exposes tools (file system access, browser control, APIs) to a Claude Code session in a standardized way, so the agent can discover and call them without bespoke scaffolding.

poster_sawyerhood.blurb: Sawyer Hood is a software engineer and entrepreneur, known for building developer tools and sharing insights on startup culture. He posts about programming, product development, and tech industry trends. His follower count is not notably large but he engages with a niche audience of builders and developers.
